en: (EĀ.Trip 2.1) "I do not perceive even a single dharma that, when uncultivated, becomes so unpliant and unwieldy as this mind.
For the mind, monks, when uncultivated, becomes unpliant and unwieldy.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: 'We shall not let our mind remain uncultivated, unpliant, and unwieldy. In this way, monks, you should train yourselves."
(EĀ.Trip 2.2) "I do not perceive even a single other dharma that, when well-cultivated, becomes so supple and workable as this mind.
For the mind, monks, when well-cultivated, becomes supple and workable.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: 'We shall cultivate the mind so that it becomes supple and indeed workable. In this way, monks, you should train yourselves."
(EĀ.Tri 2.3) "I do not perceive even a single other phenomenon that, when thus well-cultivated, becomes so supple and workable as this mind.
For the mind, monks, when well-cultivated, becomes supple and workable. Just as among all varieties of wood, sandalwood is declared to be the foremost in terms of suppleness and workability."
"In the same way, monks, I do not perceive even a single other dharma that, when well-cultivated, becomes so supple and workable as this mind.
For the mind, monks, when well-cultivated, becomes supple and workable.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: 'We shall cultivate the mind so that it will become supple and indeed workable. In this way, monks, you should train yourselves."

(EĀ.Trip 3.11) "I do not perceive even a single dharma that, when untamed, unguarded, unprotected, unrestrained, and uncultivated, results in such a bitter ripening of suffering in the future as this mind does.
For, monks, the mind— when untamed, unguarded, unprotected, unrestrained, and uncultivated— results in a bitter ripening of suffering in the future."

Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: "We shall not allow our minds to remain untamed, unguarded, unprotected, unrestrained, and uncultivated, which would result in the ripening of suffering in the future. In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.

(EĀ.Trip 3.12) “I do not perceive even a single other dharma that, when thus well-tamed, well-guarded, well-protected, well-restrained, and well-cultivated, results in such a happy ripening in the future as this mind does.
For the mind, monks, when well-tamed, well-guarded, well-protected, well-restrained, and well-cultivated, results in a happy ripening in the future.”

Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: "We shall have a mind that is well-tamed, well-guarded, well-protected, well-restrained, and well-cultivated, which will result in happiness in the future. In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
Just as there is ripening of suffering and ripening of happiness, so too [there is] for what is not beneficial and for what is beneficial,

for what is disadvantageous and for what is advantageous, for suffering and for happiness, for misfortune and for prosperity, for failure and for success, for lack of accomplishment and for accomplishment, for non-perfection and for perfection, for decline and for non-decline.
(EĀ.Trip 3.21) "I do not perceive even a single dharma that, when untamed, unguarded, unprotected, unrestrained, and uncultivated, leads to such passion as this mind does.
For, monks, the mind—when untamed, unguarded, unprotected, unrestrained, and uncultivated—leads to passion.

Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: 'We shall not allow our mind to remain untamed, unguarded, unprotected, unrestrained, and uncultivated so that it leads to passion. In this way, monks, you should train yourselves."

(EĀ.Trip 3.22) "I do not perceive even a single other dharma that, when thus well-tamed, well-guarded, well-protected, well-restrained, and well-cultivated, leads to the absence of passion as does this mind.
For the mind, monks, when well-tamed, well-guarded, well-protected, well-restrained, and well-cultivated, leads to the absence of passion."

Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: "May our mind be well-tamed, well-guarded, well-protected, well-restrained, and well-cultivated, so that it will lead to non-attachment. Monks, you should train yourselves in this way:

for the sake of attachment and non-attachment; likewise for hatred and non-hatred, delusion and non-delusion, bondage and liberation, defilement and purification, accumulation and diminution, grasping and non-grasping.

For annihilation and non-annihilation; for gathering together and dispersing; for fumigation and fanning away; for abundance and emaciation; for association and non-association; for conceptual proliferation and the absence of proliferation; for attachment and non-attachment; for lack of tranquility and tranquility.
It is just as if there were a rice awn or a barley awn that was wrongly directed;
if a delicate woman or man seeking comfort were to tread upon that awn with their feet,
it would be impossible for it to pierce the skin and draw blood.
For what reason?
Because of the false and misguided application of his own mind. Just so, alas, with a mind that is falsely and wrongly directed, he will seek to know for his own sake.

Whether for the sake of others, or for the sake of both, or whether he will know or see a superior human state, an attainment of noble distinction, or knowledge, vision, or a state of abiding in contact with it— this is impossible. Why is that?
Because the mind is wrongly and perversely directed.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: "We shall not allow our minds to become wrongly and perversely directed. In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
It is just as if there were a rice sprout or a barley sprout that had been properly planted;
and a delicate man or woman, seeking comfort, were to tread upon that sprout with their feet.
It is possible that it would pierce the skin and draw blood.
For what reason?
Because Śuka had made a perfectly correct vow.
Just so, alas, with a mind that has made a perfectly correct vow, he will know for his own sake.

Whether for the sake of others, or for the sake of both, or for the sake of a superior human state— a realization of a noble distinction beyond the ordinary— there is the possibility that he will know or see such knowledge or vision.
Why is that?
Because the mind is upright and rightly directed.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: "We shall ensure that our minds are rightly directed. In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
(EĀ.Trip 5.11) It is just as if there were a water vessel mixed with turmeric or ink, made turbid;
therein a man with sight, though examining the reflection of his own face, would not see it.
For what reason?

Because of the turbidity of the water-vessel, even so, alas, with a turbid mind he will not know for his own sake, or for the sake of another, or for the sake of both, nor will he know the higher human state,
the attainment of the distinction of the noble ones, or knowledge and vision.
It is impossible that he will know or see [the state of] dwelling in ease;
for what reason?
Because of the turbidity of the mind.
"Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: 'Our minds shall not be wrongly directed. In this way, monks, you should train yourselves."
It is just as if there were a water vessel that had not been mixed with turmeric or ink and was not turbid;
therein a man with good eyesight, examining the reflection of his own face, would see it.
For what reason?
Just as because of the clarity of the water vessel,

even so, indeed, with an untroubled mind, he will know for his own sake, or for the sake of others, or for the sake of both, or the superior human state, the attainment of the distinguished excellence of the noble ones, or knowledge or vision.
Or he will know or see the state of dwelling in comfort; this is possible.
Why is that?
Because of the clarity of the mind.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: "We shall keep our minds free from turbidity. In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
(EĀ.Trip 6.11) It is just as if there were a water vessel heated by fire, thoroughly heated, boiling, and overflowing with foam;
therein a man with sight, while examining the reflection of his own face, would not see it.
For what reason?
Because the water-vessel is turbid; even so, alas, with a turbid mind he might think he knows his own welfare, or the welfare of others,
or the welfare of both, or the superhuman state, or the attainment of the distinction of the noble ones, or knowledge, or vision.
It is impossible that he will know or see [the state of] dwelling in comfort;
for what reason?
Because of the turbidity of the mind.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: "We shall not allow our minds to become turbid. In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
(EĀ.Trip 6.21) It is just as if there were a water vessel that had not been heated by fire, nor made hot, nor stirred, and had not become turbid;
a man with good eyesight looking for the reflection of his own face therein would not see it.
For what reason?
Just as [one perceives] because the water-vessel is free from turbidity,

even so, indeed, with a mind that is free from turbidity, he will know for his own sake, or for the sake of others, or for the sake of both; or he will attain the higher human state, the noble distinction, the realization, the knowledge, or the vision.
Or he will know or see the state of dwelling in comfort; this is possible.
For what reason?
Because of the clarity of his mind.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: "We shall ensure that our minds are not turbid. In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
(EĀ.Trip 7.11) It is just as if there were a water vessel covered over with moss and duckweed;
a man with sight, while looking at the reflection of his own face, would not see it.
For what reason?
Because of the turbidity of the water-vessel, even so, alas, with a turbid mind he will not know for his own sake, or for the sake of another, or for the sake of both,
nor the higher human state, the attainment of the distinction of the noble ones, or knowledge and vision.
It is impossible that he would know or see [the state of] dwelling in ease;
for what reason?
Because of the turbidity of the mind.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: "We shall not allow our minds to become turbid. In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
It is just as if there were a water vessel that was not covered by moss or duckweed;
therein a man with sight, while examining the reflection of his own face, would see it.
For what reason?
Just as [one knows the state] of a water vessel because it is not turbid,
even so, alas, with a turbid mind he might think he will know for his own sake, or for the sake of another,
or for the sake of both, or a superior human state, or the attainment of the special distinction of the noble ones, or knowledge, or vision.
Or he will know or see the state of dwelling in comfort; this is possible.
For what reason?
Because of the clarity of the mind.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: "We shall keep our minds free from turbidity. In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
It is just as if there were a bowl of water stirred, agitated, and whirled by the wind;
in that situation, a man with sight, while examining his own facial reflection, would not see it.
For what reason?
Because the water-vessel is turbid.
In the very same way, alas, with a turbid mind he will not know his own welfare or the welfare of others.

Whether for the sake of both [heaven and liberation], or for the higher human states (*uttaramanuṣyadharma*), or for the attainment of a distinguished noble state, or for knowledge, or vision, or a state of dwelling in comfort—he will know it or he will see it; this is impossible.
Why is that?
"Because of the turbidity of the mind.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: 'We shall not allow our minds to become turbid. In this way, monks, you should train yourselves."
It is just as if there were a bowl of water that was not stirred by the wind, not agitated, not whirled about, and not moved;
and therein a man with sight, examining the reflection of his own face, would see it.
For what reason?
Because the water vessel is not turbid.
In the very same way, alas, with a turbid mind, he will seek to know either his own welfare or the welfare of others.

Or it is possible that he will know or see, for the sake of both [gods and humans], either a superior human state, or the attainment of a distinction of the noble ones, or knowledge, or vision, or a state of abiding in comfort;
for what reason? Because such a possibility exists.
Because the mind is undisturbed.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: "We shall keep our minds undisturbed. In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
It is just as if a water vessel were placed in a dark place within the range of vision;
there, a man with sight, though examining the reflection of his own face, would not see it.
For what reason?
Because the water vessel has been placed in darkness.
In the very same way, alas, with a turbid mind, he will know neither his own welfare nor the welfare of others.

Whether for the sake of both [gods and humans], or for the sake of the latter, it is impossible that he would know or see a superhuman state, a distinguished attainment of a noble one, or knowledge, vision, or a state of abiding in comfort; why is that? Because such a thing cannot exist.
Because the mind has become like darkness, therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: "We shall not allow our minds to become darkened. In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
It is just as if a water vessel were placed in a place free from darkness,
within the range of vision;
there, a man with sight, while examining the reflection of his own face, would see it.
For what reason?
Because the water vessel has been placed where there is no darkness.
In the very same way, alas, with a mind that has become free from darkness, he will know for his own sake or for the sake of others.

Or for the sake of both, or for the sake of a superior state, or for the superhuman quality (*uttara-manuṣya-dharma*), or for the attainment of the distinction of an Noble One (*alam-ārya-viśeṣādhigama*), or for knowledge, or vision, or a state of dwelling in comfort—he will know it or he will see it; this is possible.
For what reason?

Because the mind has been made free from darkness, therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: "We shall ensure that our minds are not darkened. In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
It is just as if there were a mirror that was impure, unclean, and unpolished; a man with good eyesight, while examining his own facial reflection therein, would not see it. Why is that?
Because the mirror is not pure;

even so, alas, with a mind that is impure, unpurified, and unprepared, he will not know for himself, or for another, or for both, nor will he attain the higher human states or the noble distinction of realization.
It is impossible that he will know or see either knowledge, vision, or a state of dwelling in comfort;
for what reason?
Because his mind is unpurified.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: "We shall ensure that our minds do not become impure. In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
It is just as if there were a mirror that was perfectly pure, bright, and well-polished; therein a man with sight, examining the reflection of his own face, would see it. For what reason?
Because of the extreme purity of the mirror;

even so, indeed, with a mind that is purified, cleansed, and well-prepared, he will know for his own sake, or for the sake of others, or for the sake of both, or the higher human state, which is the attainment of the distinguished qualities of the Noble Ones.
It is possible that he will know or see either knowledge, or vision, or a state of dwelling in comfort;
for what reason? Because of the utter purity of his mind.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: "We shall make our minds perfectly pure and cleansed. In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
It is just as if there were a pool of water that was agitated, churned, and turned into a turbid mass;
a man with sight, looking for the reflection of his own face therein, would not see it.
For what reason?

Just as because of the turbidity of a pool of water, even so, alas, with a turbid mind he will not know for his own sake, or for the sake of another, or for the sake of both, nor will he know the higher human state,
the attainment of the distinction of the noble ones, or knowledge or vision.
It is impossible that he will know or see [the state of] dwelling in ease;
for what reason?
Because of the turbidity of the mind.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: "We shall not allow our minds to become turbid. In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
It is just as if there were a pool of water that was clear, serene, and undisturbed;
therein a man with good eyesight, while examining the reflection of his own face, would see it.
For what reason?
Because the pool of water is undisturbed;

even so, indeed, with an undisturbed mind, he will know for his own sake, or for the sake of others, or for the sake of both, or the superior human state, the attainment of the distinction of the noble ones, or knowledge and vision.
It is possible that he will know or see a state of dwelling in comfort;
for what reason?
Because his mind is untroubled.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: "We shall keep our minds free from turbidity. In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
+ + + gap (EĀ.Trip 13.11) In a poorly proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya, he who repeatedly encourages others [to follow it] produces much evil.
It is just so: it happens as follows—that the Dharma and Vinaya are poorly expounded.
In a well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya, one who encourages others to undertake [the practice] generates much merit.
It is just so; for indeed, this Dharma and Vinaya are well-expounded.
(EĀ.Trip 13.12) In a poorly expounded Dharma and Vinaya, he who repeatedly encourages others [to adopt it] produces much evil;
thus it is, because that Dharma and Vinaya is poorly expounded.
In a well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya, one who encourages others extensively generates much merit;
it is just as it is when the Dharma and Vinaya are well-expounded.
(EĀ.Trip 13.13) In a poorly proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya, both he who encourages another to undertake [the training] and he who is encouraged to undertake it produce much demerit.
It is just so: it happens thus because the Dharma and Vinaya are poorly expounded; whereas in a well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya, one who encourages others to undertake [the training]—
And both he who is being exhorted and he who exhorts produce much merit;
this is so because the Dharma and Vinaya are well-expounded.
(EĀ.Trip 13.14) In a poorly proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya:
(a) he who encourages [others], (b) he who is encouraged, and (c) [the act of encouraging].
And whoever, having been exhorted, practices according to suchness— though they all produce much demerit—
it happens thus because the Dharma and Vinaya have been poorly proclaimed; whereas in a well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya, [it is otherwise].
He who exhorts, he who is exhorted, and he who, having been exhorted, practices in accordance with suchness— all of them produce abundant merit.
It is just so, for this Dharma and Vinaya are well-expounded.
Just as there are four sūtras by way of exhortation, so too there are four sūtras by way of acceptance.

In a poorly expounded Dharma and Vinaya, to the extent that one exerts vigor, to that same extent there is evil; in a well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya, to the extent that one is indolent, to that same extent there is evil. In a poorly expounded Dharma and Vinaya, to the extent that one is indolent, to that same extent there is excellence.
In the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya, to the extent that one exerts energy, to that same extent there is excellence.
Just as evil is [opposed to] what is beneficial, so too is suffering [opposed to] happiness;
contact is not contact with suffering.

In a poorly proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya, to whatever extent one exerts energy, to that same extent there is harm. In a well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya, to whatever extent one is indolent, to that same extent there is harm. In a poorly proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya, to whatever extent one is indolent, to that same extent there is benefit.
In the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya, to the extent that one exerts energy, to that same extent there is benefit.
Just as "non-benefit" is [the opposite of] "benefit," so too:
(EĀ.Trip 13.32–38) what is harmful, what is beneficial, suffering, happiness, misfortune, prosperity, ruin, success, failure, lack of fulfillment, fulfillment, decline, and non-decline.
(EĀ.Trip 13.41) I do not perceive even a single dharma that leads to such harm as does a poorly proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya.
A poorly proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya lead to what is disadvantageous.
I do not perceive even a single dharma that leads to such benefit as does a well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya.
A well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya lead to what is beneficial.
Just as for what is not beneficial and for what is beneficial, as previously stated.

(EĀ.Trip 13.51) I do not perceive even a single dharma by which one who is endowed with it may be known as a fool, a deluded person, an unrefined person, or an untrue man, such that one who is endowed with a poorly proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya may be known as a fool, a deluded person, an unrefined person, or an untrue man.
(EĀ.Trip 13.52) I do not perceive even a single dharma by being endowed with which a wise, discerning, and true person is to be known, as is the case with a well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya.
One who is endowed with a well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya is to be known as a wise, discerning, and true person.
A fool, however, is wounded and pierced, and is reborn as before.

As before: he goes to, falls into, and is reborn among the states of loss, the evil destinies, and the perditions; he runs and wanders through for a long duration of time. Sūtra 15.61 (EĀ.Trip 14.00): The summary verse:
There are eight evil unwholesome [actions], and likewise eight with the fetters.
The eight [stages] designated as "beings" (satva) are also [designated] by the term "eight persons" (pudgala).
The setting was Śrāvastī.
(EĀ.Trip 14.11) (a) Whatever various kinds of evil, unwholesome states arise, they all arise because of the hindrance of ignorance.
(b) Among them, the hindrance of ignorance is declared to be the foremost, namely, for the purpose of inclusion.
(a) Whatever various kinds of evil, unwholesome states arise, they all arise because of the hindrance of ignorance (*avidyā-nīvaraṇa*).

(b) Among them, the hindrance of ignorance is declared to be the foremost, namely for the purpose of inclusion. (c) When the hindrance of ignorance is destroyed, in this way their total eradication occurs.
(a) Whatever various kinds of evil, unwholesome states arise, they all arise because of the hindrance of ignorance.
(b) Among them, the hindrance of ignorance is declared to be the foremost, namely, for the purpose of inclusion.
For example: (a)
Whatever stairs there are in the gabled hall, they all lead to the peak, rest upon the peak, are connected to the peak, and converge at the peak;
the peak is declared to be their summit, namely for the purpose of gathering them together.
In the same way, whatever various kinds of evil, unwholesome states arise, they all arise because of the hindrance of ignorance.
Among them, the hindrance of ignorance is declared to be the foremost, namely, for the sake of their inclusion.
(a) Whatever various kinds of evil, unwholesome states arise, they all arise because of the hindrance of ignorance (*avidyā-nīvaraṇa*).
(b) Among them, the hindrance of ignorance is declared to be the foremost for the purpose of inclusion. (c) When the hindrance of ignorance is destroyed, their total eradication occurs in this way.
(EĀ.Trip 14.32) It is just as follows:
(a) whatever stairways there may be in a gabled hall, they all lead to the peak, rest upon the peak, are connected to the peak, and terminate at the peak;
(b) the peak is declared to be their summit, that is to say, for the purpose of gathering [them together].
(c) When the peak has been struck down, in this way their eradication occurs.
In the same way, whatever various kinds of evil, unwholesome states arise, they all arise because of the hindrance of ignorance (*avidyā-nīvaraṇa*).
Among them, the hindrance of ignorance is declared to be the foremost, namely, for the purpose of inclusion.
(c) When the hindrance of ignorance has been overcome, in this way their total eradication occurs.
It is not by any other single factor that these beings are thus obstructed;
veiled by delusion, they wander perpetually through day and night.
But having abandoned that ignorance here and shattered the mass of darkness,
he does not transmigrate again, for he possesses no cause [for rebirth].
Just as there are four discourses regarding the hindrance of ignorance, so too there are four discourses regarding the fetter of craving.
In this regard, these two verses should be spoken:
(EĀ.Trip 14.52) "Sentient beings are bound by craving, their minds stained by passion for existence and non-existence; they are yoked to Māra, those people who lack security."
They come to old age and death, just as a calf seeks its mother.
Having abandoned that craving here, free from craving for existence or non-existence,
the monk who has overcome craving through lack of desire is completely extinguished.

(EĀ.Trip 14.6) Just as there are eight sūtras beginning with "whatever various kinds of evil, unwholesome dharmas," so too there are eight sūtras beginning with "whatever various kinds of fettering dharmas.

(EĀ.Trip 14.71) I do not perceive even a single dharma endowed with which sentient beings run on and wander through for a long time—that is to say, by the hindrance of ignorance; it is because they are endowed with the hindrance of ignorance that sentient beings run on and wander through for a long time.
Having spoken this very sutra, there is an additional verse:
"It is not by means of any other single dharma that these beings,
shrouded in the darkness of delusion, wander through the cycle of existence day and night."
But having abandoned that ignorance here and shattered the mass of darkness,
he does not transmigrate again, for he possesses no further cause.

(EĀ.Trip 14.81) I do not perceive even a single dharma by which, when possessed by sentient beings wandering and transmigrating through the long course of time, the prior limit of suffering is not known— namely, the obscuration of ignorance.
For sentient beings possessed by the obscuration of ignorance, wandering and transmigrating through the long course of time, the prior limit of suffering is not known.
Having recited this very sutra, the following verse should be spoken again:
"Not by any other single dharma is this generation so obstructed that,
shrouded in the darkness of delusion, it wanders through day and night forever."
But having abandoned that ignorance here and shattered the mass of darkness,
he does not transmigrate again, for he possesses no cause [for rebirth].
(EĀ.Trip 14.91) “I do not perceive even a single dharma by being endowed with which beings run on and wander through the long course of existence—that is to say, by the fetter of craving.
It is by being endowed with the fetter of craving that beings run on and wander through the long course of existence.
Having spoken this very sutra, the verse should then be recited.
(EĀ.Trip 14.92) A person with craving as his companion wanders through this very long path;
again and again he takes up [existence], and again and again he enters the womb.
Thus, for sentient beings, there is the state of being thus and the state of being otherwise, as well as their coming and going.
But having abandoned that craving here, and having cut off the stream so difficult to cross,
he does not wander in saṃsāra again, for craving no longer exists for him.

(EĀ.Trip 14.101) I do not perceive even a single dharma by reason of which, for beings endowed with it who have run and wandered through the long course of saṃsāra, a prior limit of suffering is not known;
for beings endowed with craving who have run and wandered through the long course of saṃsāra, a prior limit of suffering is not known.
Having recited this very sutra, the following verse should be spoken: (EĀ.Trip 14.102) "With craving as his companion, a person wanders through the very long path of saṃsāra;
again and again he takes up [existence], and again and again he enters the womb."
The state of being thus, the state of being otherwise, and the coming and going of sentient beings.
But having abandoned that craving here and cut off the stream so difficult to cross,
he does not wander in saṃsāra again, for craving no longer exists for him.
Just as there are eight discourses concerning sentient beings, so too are there eight discourses concerning persons.
Summary verse:
Cause, and likewise the precursor, the root, and that which is with song;
two sets of eight, two sets of six—these should be joined with the dark fortnight.
“Monks, ignorance is the cause of passion, the cause of hatred, and the cause of delusion.
Knowledge is the cause of non-passion, the cause of non-hatred, and the cause of non-delusion.
Thus, monks, karma is the cause of rebirth, and craving is the cause of manifestation—this being so for all wholesome but tainted karma consisting of cultivation.”
The beings born there experience the ripening [of their karma];
therefore, I say that beings go according to their karma.

(EĀ.Trip 15.21) Ignorance is the precursor, the primary cause for the arising of various kinds of evil, unwholesome states; it is their accumulation, characterized by a lack of shame and a lack of dread. For what reason?
Because a monk who lacks shame and lacks dread has fallen into ignorance.
(EĀ.Trip 15.22) Wisdom is the precursor, the forerunner, for the arising of various kinds of wholesome qualities; it is accompanied by a sense of shame and a dread of blame.
Why is that?
Because a monk who possesses shame and a dread of blame has attained wisdom.
(EĀ.Trip 15.31) Whatever various kinds of evil, unwholesome states arise, they all have ignorance as their root, ignorance as their origin, ignorance as their source, and ignorance as their cause.
For whatever various kinds of evil, unwholesome states arise, monks, they have ignorance as their root.
Why is that?
For a monk who has fallen into ignorance, not knowing things as they truly are, does not understand wholesome and unwholesome states as they truly are;

he does not understand blameworthy and blameless states, those to be cultivated and those not to be cultivated, inferior and superior states, dark and bright states, and those states that arise dependently as they truly are.

Not knowing wholesome and unwholesome phenomena as they really are, not knowing blameworthy and blameless phenomena, those to be cultivated and those not to be cultivated, inferior and superior phenomena, dark and bright phenomena, and phenomena that are counterparts arising through dependent origination as they really are, one becomes possessed by ignorance.

(EĀ.Trip 15.32) Whatever various kinds of wholesome qualities (*kuśala-dharma*) arise, they all have knowledge (*vidyā*) as their root, originate from knowledge, are of the same nature as knowledge, and are produced by knowledge. For whatever various kinds of wholesome qualities arise, monks, they have knowledge as their root.
Why is that?

For a monk who has attained knowledge, knowing things as they truly are, understands wholesome and unwholesome phenomena; he understands as they truly are blameworthy and blameless phenomena, those to be cultivated and those not to be cultivated, inferior and superior phenomena, dark and bright phenomena, and phenomena that are counterparts and dependently originated.

Knowing wholesome and unwholesome phenomena as they really are— knowing them as blameworthy and blameless, as those to be cultivated and those not to be cultivated, as inferior and superior, as dark and bright, and as phenomena arisen through dependent origination— one becomes possessed of true knowledge. Having spoken the sutra in this way, the verses should be recited.
Whatever miserable states there may be in this world and the next,
they all have ignorance as their root and are brought about by desire and greed.
When one becomes desirous of evil through evil conduct and sphere of activity,
then that person produces evil, by which he goes to the states of woe.
Therefore, by fading away from greed, hatred, and ignorance,
and by generating true knowledge, a monk shall attain the destruction of suffering.
(EĀ.Trip 15.51) I do not perceive even a single dharma that leads to such disadvantage as this: namely, the hindrance of ignorance (*avidyā-nīvaraṇa*).
The hindrance of ignorance leads to disadvantage;
and just as it leads to disadvantage, so too does it lead to what is harmful, to suffering, to calamity, to misfortune, to lack of success, to non-fulfillment, and to decline.
(EĀ.Trip 15.51) Just as the dark side [of existence] is defined by the hindrance of ignorance (*avidyā-nīvaraṇa*), so too is the dark side defined by the fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*).

(EĀ.Trip 15.61) I do not perceive even a single dharma by the possession of which a person may be known as a fool, a deluded one, an unclarified one, or an untrue man, such as by the hindrance of ignorance.
One who is possessed of the hindrance of ignorance should be known as a fool, a deluded one, an unclarified one, and an untrue man.
The fool, wounded by the arrow [of craving], is reborn in states of woe, miserable destinies, and perdition; he goes, falls, and is reborn there, wandering and transmigrating for a long duration.
Just as the dark side [of existence] occurs through the obscuration of ignorance, so too does the dark side occur through the fetter of craving.
The summary verse: The arising of the five hindrances, the reversal of man and woman, and likewise that which is done by both; thus is this chapter here proclaimed.

(EĀ.Trip 16.101) I do not perceive even a single dharma by which the hindrance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa*), unarisen, arises, or having arisen, goes to further increase, growth, and expansion, as happens when the meditation on the foul (*aśubhā*) is not practiced, not cultivated, and not made much of.

When the meditation on the foul is not practiced, not cultivated, and not made much of, the hindrance of sensual desire that has not yet arisen arises, and that which has already arisen increases, grows, and becomes extensive.
(EĀ.Trip 16.102) I do not perceive even a single dharma by which the hindrance of ill will that has not yet arisen arises,
and that which has already arisen increases, grows, and becomes extensive, as does [the hindrance of ill will] when loving-kindness is not practiced.
Through not cultivating, not frequently practicing,

not habituating, not developing, and not making much of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), the hindrance of ill-will (*vyāpāda-nīvaraṇa*) arises if it has not yet arisen, and if it has already arisen, it increases, grows, and reaches full expansion.
(EĀ.Trip 16.103) I do not perceive even a single dharma by which the hindrance of sloth and torpor (*styāna-middha-nīvaraṇa*), if it has not yet arisen, [arises]...
It arises, and having arisen, it proceeds toward further existence, increase, and expansion, just as [it would] through not being practiced, not being cultivated, and not being made much of;
[likewise] through not being practiced, not being cultivated, and not being made much of.
The hindrance of sloth and torpor that has not yet arisen arises, and that which has already arisen increases, grows, and becomes expansive.

(EĀ.Trip 16.104) I do not perceive even a single dharma by which the hindrance of restlessness and remorse that has not yet arisen arises, and that which has already arisen increases, grows, and becomes expansive, as does [the hindrance of sloth and torpor] through the lack of *śamatha*.

When calm abiding has not been practiced, cultivated, and frequently developed, the hindrance of sloth and torpor arises if it has not yet arisen, and once arisen, it increases, grows, and expands further. (EĀ.Trip 16.105) I do not perceive even a single dharma by which the hindrance of doubt, if not yet arisen, arises... (SHT 974aR2)

And that which has arisen goes toward further increase, growth, and expansion, just as through the non-cultivation, non-development, and non-repetition of the investigation into dependent origination according to specific conditionality (*idaṃpratyayatā-pratītyasamutpāda*). Through the non-cultivation, non-development, and non-repetition of the investigation into dependent origination according to specific conditionality, the hindrance of doubt (*vicikitsā-nīvaraṇa*) that has not yet arisen arises, and that which has arisen goes toward further increase, growth, and expansion.

(EĀ.Trip 16.106) I do not perceive even a single dharma by which the hindrance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa*) that has not yet arisen does not arise, and that which has already arisen is abandoned, as [it occurs] when the beautiful (*śubhā*) is practiced, cultivated, and frequently practiced. When the beautiful is practiced, cultivated, and frequently practiced, the hindrance of sensual desire does not arise, and that which has already arisen is abandoned.

(EĀ.Trip 16.107) I do not perceive even a single dharma by which the hindrance of ill-will (*vyāpāda-nīvaraṇa*), when unarisen, does not arise, and when arisen, is abandoned, as is the case with loving-kindness (*maitrī*) when it is practiced,
cultivated, and frequently practiced. When loving-kindness is practiced, cultivated, and frequently practiced, the hindrance of ill-will does not arise, and when it has arisen, it is abandoned.
(EĀ.Trip 16.108) I do not perceive even a single dharma by which the unarisen hindrance of sloth and torpor does not arise, and the arisen [hindrance] is abandoned,
as it is when [this practice] is cultivated, developed, and practiced frequently.
When this is cultivated, developed, and practiced frequently, the hindrance of sloth and torpor does not arise, and the arisen [hindrance] is abandoned.

(EĀ.Trip 16.109) I do not perceive even a single dharma by which the hindrance of restlessness and remorse that has not yet arisen does not arise, and that which has already arisen is abandoned, as is the case with *śamatha* when it is practiced,

cultivated, and frequently practiced. When *śamatha* is practiced, cultivated, and frequently practiced, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse does not arise, and that which has already arisen is abandoned.
(I do not perceive even a single dharma by which the hindrance of doubt that has not yet arisen does not arise,

and that which has already arisen is abandoned, as occurs through the investigation of specific conditionality and dependent origination when it has been practiced, cultivated, and frequently developed.)

Through the investigation of dependent origination as specific conditionality—when it has been practiced, cultivated, and frequently developed—the hindrance of doubt does not arise, and that which has already arisen is abandoned.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: "In this way, no hindrance shall arise in us, and that which has arisen shall be abandoned. In this manner, monks, you should train yourselves.

(EĀ.Trip 16.2–17.3) Not extant (EĀ.Trip 17.41): "I do not perceive even a single dharma by which unarisen wholesome dharmas do not arise, arisen [wholesome dharmas] are abandoned, unarisen unwholesome dharmas arise, and arisen [unwholesome dharmas]..."
They undergo further increase, growth, and expansion through association with evil friends, companionship with the wicked, and contact with the unwholesome.
For what reason?
Because for a monk who dwells with an evil friend, with wicked companions, and in the company of the unwholesome, wholesome states that have not yet arisen...
Dharmas do not arise, and those that have arisen are abandoned; evil, unwholesome dharmas that have not yet arisen do arise, and those that have arisen go to further increase, growth, and expansion.

(EĀ.Trip 17.42) I do not perceive even a single dharma by which unarisen evil and unwholesome states do not arise, and those already arisen are abandoned; and by which unarisen wholesome states arise, and those already arisen proceed toward further increase, growth, and expansion— just as occurs through having virtuous friends, virtuous companions, and virtuous associations.
For what reason?

Because for a monk who dwells with a spiritual friend, with virtuous companions, and in association with the virtuous, unarisen evil and unwholesome states do not arise, and those that have arisen are abandoned; likewise, unarisen wholesome states [arise].
They arise, and having arisen, they proceed to further existence, increase, and expansion.

Just as it is with bad friendship and good friendship, so it is with improper mental attention and proper mental attention; likewise with laziness and the exertion of vigor, heedlessness and heedfulness, and false view and right view.
False view is the foremost of faults.
For what reason?
Because for a person who holds false views, whatever bodily action, whatever vocal action, or whatever volition there is, [all proceed] from that same false view.

Whatever prayers, whatever vows, and whatever formative predispositions he has, all those qualities of his lead to what is undesirable, to what is unlovely, to what is unpleasant, to what is disagreeable, to what is unpleasing, and to what is unwanted. For what reason?
For a view is indeed evil, namely, wrong view.

Just as, monks, bitter seeds of bottle-gourd, or seeds of the neem tree, or seeds of the kāśātakī plant might be sown in a fertile field or planted in a very moist region of earth; whatever [they encounter]—

In this way, they take from the earth the essence of the earth, from water the essence of water, from fire the essence of fire, and from wind the essence of wind; all these essences of his turn toward bitterness, pungency, and lack of flavor.
For what reason?
For seeds that are bitter, pungent, and tasteless— just so, monks, wrong view is the foremost of blameworthy things.
Whatever bodily action, whatever vocal action, or whatever volition belongs to a person who holds wrong view and acts according to such a view [is likewise foremost among blameworthy things].
Whatever prayers, whatever vows, and whatever formative activities he has performed— all those qualities of his lead to what is undesirable,
to what is unlovely, to what is unpleasant, to what is disagreeable, to what is unpleasing, and to what is unwanted. Why is that?
For views, monks, are evil, namely, wrong view. Right view, monks, is supreme among blameless things.
And why is that?

For a person endowed with right view, whatever bodily action they perform, whatever vocal action they perform, whatever volition, whatever aspiration, whatever resolve, and whatever formative factors (saṃskāra) there are— all those qualities of theirs lead to what is desired, to what is lovely, to what is dear, to what is agreeable, to what is pleasing, and to what is intended.
For what reason?
Monks, a view is indeed auspicious, namely, right view.
It is just as if seeds of sugarcane, or seeds of rice, or seeds of grapes were sown in a fertile field.

If they were placed on a very moist region of the earth, whatever essence of the earth they take from the earth, the essence of water from the waters, the essence of fire from fire, or the essence of wind from the wind— all those essences of his would result in being non-bitter, non-pungent, and sweet.
For what reason?
Because seeds that are not bitter, not pungent, and sweet are indeed excellent;
in the same way, right view is supreme among blameless things.
For what reason? Because for a person endowed with right view, whatever bodily action, whatever verbal action, whatever volition,
whatever aspiration, whatever vow, and whatever formative forces there may be— all those qualities of theirs lead to what is desirable.
They conduce to being lovely, to being dear, to being agreeable, to being pleasing, and to being desirable.
For what reason?
Because, monks, a view that is auspicious is indeed right view.
One should not cultivate base qualities, nor dwell in negligence;
one should not take pleasure in wrong views, nor become one who increases the world [of suffering].
Whoever possesses even a superior degree of mundane right view does not go to an evil rebirth for thousands of births, even though they are numerous.

The summary verse: Harmfulness, giving, immorality, morality, the two mental [actions], merit, and likewise the eightfold [path]— having made these, there are fourteen [sections] including the destructive ones.

(EĀ.Trip 18.11) One single dharma arises in the world for the harm of many people, for the suffering of many people, for the disadvantage, harm, and suffering of gods and humans; that is to say, stinginess (*mātsarya*).
Stinginess arises in the world for the harm of many people, for the suffering of many people, for the disadvantage, harm, and suffering of gods and humans.

(EĀ.Trip 18.12) One single dharma arises in the world for the benefit of many people, for the happiness of many people, out of compassion for the world, for the advantage, benefit, and happiness of gods and humans; that is to say, the absence of the stain of stinginess.

Free from the stain of stinginess, he appears in the world for the benefit of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, and for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of gods and humans.
(EĀ.Trip 18.2) In the *Dānasūtra* (EĀ.Trip 18.21):

"For in this way beings would come to know the fruit of giving and the ripening of the fruit of the distribution of gifts, just as I know the fruit of giving and the ripening of the fruit of the distribution of gifts."
Is it even now that this very last morsel of food exists?
Edible food.

They should not consume even the very last morsel without having first eaten it or shared it, provided that they find a worthy recipient to receive it; nor should the stain of stinginess arise in them and persist, completely overwhelming their minds.

For this reason, sentient beings do not know the fruit of giving, nor the ripening of the fruit of sharing gifts, in the way that I know the fruit of giving and the ripening of the fruit of sharing gifts.
And they do not give or share the fruit of their ripening; therefore, they enjoy it with a grasping mind,
and the state of stinginess that has arisen in them persists, completely taking possession of their hearts.
In this way indeed would beings understand, as it was proclaimed by the Great Seer:
how the ripening of sharing becomes of great benefit.
They should not consume [food] without having given it away, nor should they be stingy; nor should a mind of attachment arise in them in any way whatsoever.
Because these fools, shrouded by the darkness of delusion, do not understand this, they eat without having given; therefore, with a mind full of grasping,
the thought of stinginess arises and remains, seizing their hearts.
For in this way, beings would know their own destination, rebirth, and future state as those who are immoral and of evil nature—
just as I know the destination, rebirth, and future state of beings who are immoral and of evil nature.
Even now they might wither or dry up, like green reeds or grass covered by a spider’s web.
But because beings who are immoral and of evil character do not know their own destiny, rebirth, and future state, they therefore practice misconduct with body, speech, and mind.

Having practiced misconduct with the body, and having practiced misconduct with speech and mind, they—on account of that cause and by reason of that condition—after the breaking up of the body, after death, are reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, in the hells.
Thus indeed would beings know, as it was spoken by the Great Seer:
"The destiny of those of evil deeds and immoral conduct after passing away from here."
They would wither or dry up, like green reeds or spiderwebs;
yet fools, shrouded in the darkness of delusion, do not understand this.
Therefore, those who are unrestrained in body, speech, and mind perform evil deeds which result in bitter consequences.
That action is not well done which, having been performed, one regrets;
it is an action whose ripening one experiences while weeping with a tearful face.
In this regard, one who has performed a deed well, having done it rightly, does not feel regret;
being satisfied and of good cheer, he experiences its ripening.

In this way, indeed, beings would know: "Those who are virtuous, endowed with qualities, gentle, and possessed of wholesome dharmas— just as I know the destination, rebirth, and future state of beings who are virtuous, endowed with qualities, gentle, and possessed of wholesome dharmas— they too shall know their own destination, rebirth, and future state."

Now, even on account of this putrid body, being born, being ashamed, being weary, and being disgusted, people might take up weapons, consume poison, hang themselves with ropes, or throw themselves from precipices.
In this way, indeed, beings would understand what has been proclaimed by the Great Seer:
the destination of those endowed with ethical conduct, and the destination of those who live according to the Dharma.
Those who delight in the world of the gods, being born again and again with this putrid body, would even wield weapons against one another.

(EĀ.Trip 18.51) Whether it be a woman or a man who is immoral and of evil character, possessed of misconduct of body and possessed of misconduct of speech and mind— at the breaking up of that body, such a mind-made body as this is produced for him, resembling the luster of a black woolen blanket or the darkness of a night of deep gloom.
Those whose divine eye is perfectly pure see him.

(EĀ.Trip 18.52) Whether it be a woman or a man who is virtuous and of excellent character, yet endowed with misconduct of body but endowed with good conduct of speech and mind— at the breaking up of that body, for them, a mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*) of such a form is produced, like the luster of a white cloth or the radiance of a moonlit night. For those...
With their perfectly purified divine eye, they see him.
“Monks, do not fear meritorious deeds.
For what reason?
‘Meritorious deeds’ is a designation for that which is pleasant, desirable, lovely, dear, and agreeable.”
But you, monks, desist from demerit.
For what reason?
"Demerit" is a designation for that which is suffering—undesirable, unlovely, unpleasant, and disagreeable.
“Monks, I recall that for a long time I have experienced the ripening of merits performed over a long period—desirable, beloved, and pleasing results.
Having cultivated a mind of loving-kindness for seven years, I did not return to this world for seven eons of dissolution and evolution.
When the world was dissolving, I was reborn in the Ābhāsvara realm of the gods.”
When the world was dissolving and the Brahma palace was empty, I was reborn there.
There I became Brahmā, the Great Brahmā, the conqueror unconquered, the wielder of power over ten hundred others, the Great Brahmā, declared the foremost among those beings.
And twenty-six times I was Śakra, the lord of the gods.

And many hundreds of times I was a wheel-turning monarch, a conqueror of the four quarters, righteous, a king of dharma, endowed with the seven treasures. For me, these were the seven treasures of such a kind, namely:
the wheel-treasure, the elephant-treasure, the horse-treasure, the jewel-treasure, the woman-treasure, and the householder-treasure.
The seventh treasure was indeed the counselor-treasure, and I possessed a full thousand sons— heroic, brave, handsome in form, and crushers of enemy armies.

Having conquered this entire great earth, bounded by the ocean, in its entirety— free from thorns, free from oppression, and without punishment or weapons, but through righteousness and impartiality— I have established myself therein.
This thought occurred to me:
"Of what action is this the fruit? Of what action is this the ripening of the fruit, by which I am now so possessed of great psychic power and so possessed of great majesty?
This thought occurred to me.
This is the fruit of these three actions, this is the ripening of the fruit of these three actions, by which I am now so greatly powerful and so greatly majestic. Which three?
Namely, those of giving, self-restraint, and self-control.
Behold the ripening of meritorious and wholesome deeds for those who seek happiness:
having cultivated a mind of loving-kindness for seven years, O monks, I did not come to this world for seven cycles of dissolution and evolution. I did not return.
When this world was dissolving, I went to the Ābhāsvara realm; and when it was evolving, I became one who approached Brahmā. Formerly, seven times I was Mahābrahmā, possessing sovereign power.
And thirty-six times he exercised sovereignty over the gods;
and many hundreds of times he was a powerful king.
(4) At that time, he was a consecrated Kṣatriya, the lord of Jambūṣaṇḍa.
Having conquered this earth without punishment and without weapons,
he governed it rightly through non-violent Dharma;
having set in motion the Wheel of Dharma upon this circle of the earth.

I was born into such a family, possessing great wealth and vast enjoyments, endowed with every kind of property and the seven precious gems. With abundant riches and resources, I became a powerful king.
For this is the cause by which greatness and sovereignty are born. The Buddhas are the gatherers in the world; this has been well-taught by them.
Who, having heard this, would not have faith—even one of dark birth? (8–9)
Therefore, one who desires their own welfare in this world and aspires to greatness, remembering the teaching of the Buddha, should hold the true Dharma in high esteem. (10)
[They] are intent upon passion, intent upon hatred, and intent upon delusion;
[but those who are] not intent upon passion, not intent upon hatred, and not intent upon delusion.
They have not set out for the destruction of lust, nor for the destruction of hatred, nor for the destruction of delusion;
rather, they have set out for the destruction of lust, and they have set out for the destruction of hatred and the destruction of delusion.
They have not set out for the abandoning of lust, nor for the abandoning of hatred, nor for the abandoning of delusion;
rather, they have set out for the abandoning of lust, for the abandoning of hatred, and for the abandoning of delusion.

They have not set out for the sake of reaching the culmination of the removal of passion, nor for the sake of reaching the culmination of the removal of hatred, nor for the sake of reaching the culmination of the removal of delusion.

They have set out for the sake of reaching the culmination of the removal of passion, they have set out for the sake of reaching the culmination of the removal of hatred, and they have set out for the sake of reaching the culmination of the removal of delusion.
(Not endowed with virtue, not endowed with concentration, not endowed with wisdom;
[but rather] endowed with virtue, endowed with concentration, and endowed with wisdom.)
The summary verse:
Through the destruction and abandonment of passion, and through the culmination of discipline,
as well as by means of both, this chapter has been proclaimed here.
Summary verse:
And those who apply themselves with zeal,
there are two modes of discourse, two factors of the path, and the ninth is the perfection of ethical discipline.
"Monks, I shall teach you about the unrighteous assembly and the righteous assembly.
Listen to this, attend to it well and thoroughly, and I will speak.
What is the unrighteous assembly?"

Whatever assembly there may be that consists of those who take life, those who take what is not given, those who engage in sexual misconduct, and those who indulge in fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants which are the basis for negligence—
this is called an unrighteous assembly. What is a righteous assembly?

This assembly which abstains from taking life, from taking what is not given, from sexual misconduct, and from the occasion of negligence consisting in fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants—
this is called a righteous assembly (*dhārmikī parṣad*). As for what I said to you, "I shall describe to you both the unrighteous assembly and the righteous assembly," this is my response to that.
Likewise, [there are those who are] speakers of falsehood, speakers of slander, speakers of harsh words, and speakers of idle chatter;
[and there are those who] abstain from false speech, abstain from slander, abstain from harsh speech, and abstain from idle chatter.
Out of desire they go to a wrong course; out of hatred, delusion, or fear they go to a wrong course.
They do not go to a wrong course out of desire, nor out of hatred, nor out of delusion, nor out of fear.

Without investigating and without fathoming, he speaks praise of one who does not deserve praise, and he speaks dispraise of one who deserves praise; he places his confidence in a matter that does not inspire confidence, and he does not place his confidence in a matter that inspires confidence.

Having investigated and having fathomed, he speaks dispraise of one who does not deserve praise, and he speaks praise of one who deserves praise; he does not place his confidence in a matter that does not inspire confidence, and he places his confidence in a matter that inspires confidence.
Speaking of what has not been seen as having been seen; speaking of what has not been heard, not been thought, and not been cognized as having been cognized.
Speaking of what has not been seen as not having been seen; speaking of what has not been heard, not been thought, and not been cognized as not having been cognized.
One who speaks of the unseen regarding what is seen, of the unheard regarding what is heard, of the unthought regarding what is thought, and of the unknown regarding what is cognized;
one who speaks of the seen regarding what is seen, of the heard regarding what is heard, of the thought regarding what is thought, and of the cognized regarding what is cognized.
Those with wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, and wrong action;
those with right view, right intention, right speech, and right action.
Wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong concentration;
right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
They were not endowed with ethical discipline, nor endowed with concentration, nor endowed with wisdom, nor endowed with liberation;
[rather,] they were endowed with ethical discipline, endowed with concentration, endowed with wisdom, and endowed with liberation.
The summary verse:
There are five training rules, as well as the faculties, the powers, and the perfection of faith and ethical conduct.
(I shall explain to you both the unrighteous assembly and the righteous assembly.
Listen to that; attend to it well and thoroughly, and I will speak.
What is the unrighteous assembly?

Whatever assembly there may be that consists of those who take life, those who take what is not given, those who engage in sexual misconduct, those who speak falsehoods, and those who indulge in fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants which are the basis for negligence—
this is called an unrighteous assembly. What is a righteous assembly?

This assembly which abstains from taking life, abstains from taking what is not given, abstains from sexual misconduct, and abstains from fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants which are the basis for negligence—
this is called a righteous assembly (*dhārmikī parṣat*). As for what I said to you— that I would explain to you both the unrighteous assembly and the righteous assembly— this is my response to that.
Thus, they are not endowed with the faculty of faith, nor with the faculty of energy, nor with the faculty of mindfulness, nor with the faculty of concentration, nor with the faculty of wisdom;
[rather,] they are endowed with the faculty of faith, and endowed with the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom.
They were not endowed with the power of faith, nor with the power of energy, nor with the power of mindfulness, nor with the power of concentration, nor with the power of wisdom;
yet they were endowed with the power of faith, endowed with the power of energy, endowed with the power of mindfulness, endowed with the power of concentration, and endowed with the power of wisdom.
They were not perfected in faith, not perfected in ethical conduct, not perfected in learning, not perfected in relinquishment, and not perfected in wisdom.
They were endowed with faith, endowed with ethical discipline, endowed with learning, endowed with generosity, and endowed with wisdom.
(They were) not endowed with virtue, not endowed with concentration, not endowed with wisdom, not endowed with liberation, and not endowed with the knowledge and vision of liberation;
[but rather] they were endowed with virtue, endowed with concentration, endowed with wisdom, endowed with liberation, and endowed with the knowledge and vision of liberation.
Summary verse: Morality, wealth, strength, the faithful, the factors for enjoying the Dharma,
views, training, modes of discourse, the factors of the path, the factors of the way, and the illumination of the Dharma.
(I shall teach you) both the unrighteous assembly and the righteous assembly.
Listen to that; attend to it well and thoroughly, and I shall speak.
What is the unrighteous assembly?

This assembly which consists of those who take life, those who take what is not given, those who engage in sexual misconduct, those who speak falsehoods, and those who indulge in fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants that cause negligence—
this is called an unrighteous assembly. What is a righteous assembly?

This assembly which abstains from taking life, from taking what is not given, from sexual misconduct, and from the use of fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants— which are the basis for negligence—
is called a righteous assembly (*dhārmikī parṣad*). As for what I said to you— that I would teach you both the unrighteous assembly and the righteous assembly— this is my response to that.

Thus, they are not endowed with the wealth of faith, nor with the wealth of ethical conduct, nor with the wealth of moral shame, nor with the wealth of dread of blame, nor with the wealth of learning, nor with the wealth of relinquishment, nor with the wealth of wisdom.

They were endowed with the wealth of faith, the wealth of ethical discipline, the wealth of moral shame, the wealth of dread of blame, the wealth of learning, the wealth of relinquishment, and the wealth of wisdom.

They were not endowed with the power of faith, nor with the power of energy, nor with the power of moral shame, nor with the power of dread of blame, nor with the power of mindfulness, nor with the power of concentration, nor with the power of wisdom;

yet they were endowed with the power of faith, endowed with the power of energy, the power of moral shame, the power of dread of blame, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom.
(Lacking faith, shameless, without a sense of propriety, lazy, with stolen mindfulness, unconcentrated, and of poor wisdom;
possessing faith, having shame, having a sense of propriety, exerting vigor, with established mindfulness, concentrated, and endowed with wisdom.

Not knowing the Dharma, not knowing the meaning, not knowing the proper time, not knowing moderation, not knowing oneself, not knowing the assembly, and not knowing the superior or inferior qualities of individuals.

He is a knower of the Dharma, a knower of the meaning, a knower of the proper time, a knower of measure, a knower of himself, a knower of assemblies, and a knower of the superior and inferior qualities of individuals.
They are not endowed with the factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness, nor with the factor of enlightenment that is the investigation of phenomena,

nor with the factor of enlightenment that is energy, nor with the factor of enlightenment that is joy, nor with the factor of enlightenment that is tranquility, nor with the factor of enlightenment that is concentration, nor with the factor of enlightenment that is equanimity.

They are endowed with the factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness, the factor of enlightenment that is the investigation of phenomena, the factor of enlightenment that is energy, the factor of enlightenment that is joy, the factor of enlightenment that is tranquility, the factor of enlightenment that is concentration, and the factor of enlightenment that is equanimity.
(Wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness;
right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness.)

They were killers of living beings, takers of what was not given, practitioners of sexual misconduct, consumers of fermented and distilled liquors leading to negligence, speakers of falsehoods, slanderers, harsh-speakers, and idle chatterers.

They abstained from killing living beings, from taking what was not given, from sexual misconduct, from consuming fermented and distilled liquors leading to negligence, from false speech, from slander, from harsh speech, and from idle chatter. They spoke of what they had seen as having been seen; they spoke of what they had heard, sensed, or known as having been heard, sensed, or known.

One who speaks of what has not been seen regarding what has been seen; one who speaks of what has not been heard, not been thought, and not been known regarding what has been heard, thought, and known; one who speaks of what has not been seen regarding what has not been seen; one who speaks of what has not been heard, not been thought, and not been known regarding what has not been heard, thought, and known;
one who speaks of what has been seen regarding what has been seen; one who speaks of what has been heard, thought, and known regarding what has been heard, thought, and known.
(EĀ.Trip 25.10) Those with wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong concentration;
those with right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.

(Āgama 25.11) Those who take life, those who take what is not given, those who engage in sexual misconduct, those who indulge in fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants which are the basis for negligence,

those who speak falsehoods, those who speak divisively, those who speak harshly, those who engage in idle chatter, those who are covetous, those with malevolent minds, and those with wrong views; [and those] who abstain from taking life, from taking what is not given, from sexual misconduct, from fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants which are the basis for negligence, from speaking falsehoods, from divisive speech, from harsh speech, from idle chatter, and who are free from covetousness...
With a mind free from malice, they possess right view.

Those with wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, wrong concentration, and wrong liberation; and those with right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration, and right liberation; those with wrong knowledge and those with right knowledge.

(EĀ.Trip 25.13) He explains what is non-Dharma as Dharma, and what is Dharma as non-Dharma; what is non-discipline as discipline, and what is discipline as non-discipline; an offense as no offense, and no offense as an offense; a heavy [offense] as light, and a light [offense] as heavy;
one with remainder as without remainder, and one without remainder as with remainder; and what has been practiced as not practiced, and what has not been practiced as practiced.

He illuminates what has not been practiced as practiced, and what has been practiced as not practiced; what has not been spoken as spoken, and what has been spoken as not spoken; the wishless as wished for, and the wished for as wishless; the unproclaimed as proclaimed, and the proclaimed as unproclaimed; the non-encountered as encountered, and the encountered as non-encountered; and he illuminates what is not Dharma as Dharma, and what is Dharma as not Dharma, and the non-discipline as discipline.

He understands non-discipline as non-discipline and discipline as discipline; he understands an offense as an offense and a non-offense as a non-offense; he understands a grave [offense] as grave and a light [offense] as light; he understands what is with remainder as with remainder and what is without remainder as without remainder; he understands what has been practiced as practiced and what has not been practiced as not practiced;
he understands what has been spoken as spoken and what has not been spoken as not spoken; and he understands what has not been prescribed as not prescribed.

That which is intended, as intended; that which is non-designated, as non-designated; that which is designated, as designated; that which is not brought together, as not brought together; and that which is brought together, as brought together.
The summary verse:
Astringent, full of disputes, discordant, superficial, and heavy with worldly gain; uneven and ignoble—these seven qualities one should apply according to the Dharma and non-Dharma.

(EĀ.Trip 26.11) "And I shall teach you, monks, the dregs of the assembly (*parṣat-kaṣāya*) and the essence of the assembly (*parṣan-maṇḍa*). Listen to that well and attend to it thoroughly; I shall speak.
(EĀ.Trip 26.12) "What is the dregs of the assembly?
It is that assembly in which non-Dharma (*adharma*) is exalted and Dharma (*dharma*) is rejected; in which non-discipline (*avinaya*) is exalted and discipline (*vinaya*) is rejected."

Indeed, when what is non-Dharma shines forth and Dharma is obstructed; when what is non-discipline shines forth and discipline is obstructed—then individuals who speak of non-Dharma and speak of non-discipline become powerful, while individuals who speak of Dharma and speak of discipline become weak.
When those who speak of non-Dharma and speak of non-discipline are powerful, [those] who speak of Dharma...
Those individuals who advocate for discipline remain silent or, having risen, depart;
this is called the dregs of the assembly (*parṣat-kaṣāya*).
What is the essence of the assembly (*parṣan-maṇḍa*)?
In whatever assembly the Dharma shines and non-Dharma is refuted, and the Vinaya shines and non-Vinaya is refuted— indeed,
while the Dharma shines and non-Dharma is refuted, and the Vinaya shines and non-Vinaya is refuted—
the persons who speak according to the Dharma and speak according to the Vinaya become powerful, whereas those who speak against the Dharma and speak against the Vinaya do not.

When individuals are weak among those who speak according to the Dharma and those who speak according to the Vinaya, while powerful individuals speak what is not the Dharma and speak contrary to the Vinaya, such individuals either resort to the borderlands or cease to exist altogether. This is called the "scum of the assembly."
And when I said to you, "I shall teach you the corruption of the assembly and the essence of the assembly," this is what was spoken in response to that.
(I shall teach you how this assembly is without a superior and how it possesses a superior.
Listen to that; attend to it well and thoroughly, and I shall speak.
What is the assembly without a superior?

In that assembly, the junior monks dwell without respect toward the senior monks, lacking deference and not remaining under their control; and the senior monks become lax and indulgent, taking the lead in what should be avoided, casting off the burden of seclusion, and possessing little reverence for the training.
This is called an assembly that is without a leader.
What is an assembly that has a leader?
It is an assembly in which the junior monks dwell with reverence and deference toward the elder monks.

The elder monks who abide under the power of fear do not become lax, nor do they become indulgent; they have laid down their burden regarding what is to be entered upon, they are foremost in seclusion, and they possess intense reverence for the training. This is called the assembly that possesses the foremost.
And as for what was said by me, "I shall teach you an assembly that is without a superior and one that possesses a superior," this is my response to that.
(I shall teach you) both the discordant assembly and the harmonious assembly; listen to this well and attend to it thoroughly, and I shall speak.
What is the discordant assembly?
That assembly which dwells having become quarrelsome, contentious, disputatious, and fallen into strife— this is called a divided assembly. What is a harmonious assembly?
This assembly which dwells having arisen from quarreling, yet not having arisen from brawling, not being divided, and not having fallen into dispute— this is called a harmonious assembly.
As for what was said by me, "I shall teach you how an assembly that is discordant may become harmonious," this is my response to that.
(I shall teach you) both the superficial assembly and the profound one; listen to that well and attend to it thoroughly, and I shall speak.
What is the superficial assembly?
That assembly which is agitated, haughty, fickle, talkative, impudent, with impaired mindfulness, and unconcentrated—
this is called a shallow assembly. What is a profound assembly?
This assembly which is not agitated, not haughty, not fickle, not noisy, not arrogant, established in mindfulness,
and concentrated— this is called a profound assembly.
As for what was said by me, "I shall teach you both the shallow assembly and the profound assembly," this is my response to that.
(EĀ.Trip 26.51) I shall teach you concerning an assembly that values material things and one that values the Dharma; listen to this well and attend to it thoroughly, and I will speak.
(EĀ.Trip 26.52) What is an assembly that values material things?
Just as here some individuals, for the sake of material gain, honor, revere, respect, and worship one another; yet,
having placed that very material gain between them, they hack at one another, cut one another down, and completely carve one another up— even now making families destitute of their inheritance.
This is called an assembly that values material things.
What is an assembly that values the Dharma?
It is when certain individuals here, for the sake of the Dharma, honor, revere, respect, and worship one another.
Placing the Dharma alone between them, they do not chip, hack, or carve at one another, nor do they bring about the ruin of families;
this is called an assembly that values the Dharma.
"And as for what was said by me: 'I shall teach you an assembly that values material things and one that values the Dharma'—this is my response to that."
(I shall teach you how to make) this uneven assembly even; listen to that well and attend to it thoroughly, and I will speak.
What is an uneven assembly?

For example, there is a certain person here who is unrighteous and a speaker of unrighteousness; his assembly is likewise unrighteous and a speaker of unrighteousness. In the presence of his own assembly, he declares and proclaims his own doctrine through what is false, untrue, and conducive to harm.
He sets it forth, analyzes it, explains it, clarifies it, teaches it, and illuminates it; he even speaks with systematic continuity.

He points out, designates, sets forth, analyzes, explains, clarifies, teaches, and illuminates the vulnerabilities, the flaws, the variegated, and the mottled defects of the arguments of others—[defects] consisting of what is untrue, what is not so, and what is connected with what is harmful.
He speaks even with continuity;
this is called an uneven assembly. What is a level assembly?
For example, here a certain person is righteous and speaks according to the Dharma;
his assembly is also righteous and speaks according to the Dharma. In the presence of his own assembly, he explains and proclaims his own doctrine with what is real, true, and conducive to the goal.
He sets it forth, analyzes it, explains it, clarifies it, teaches it, and fully illuminates it; he even speaks with systematic connection.

He points out, designates, sets forth, analyzes, explains, clarifies, teaches, and fully illuminates the vulnerabilities, the flaws, the variegated, and the mottled aspects of the arguments of others, by means of what is real, what is true, and what is endowed with meaning.
He speaks with continuity;
this is called an even assembly.
As for what I said—that I shall teach you the uneven assembly as even—this is my response to that.
(I shall teach you) both the ignoble assembly and the noble assembly; listen to that well and attend to it thoroughly, and I shall speak.
(EĀ.Trip 26.72) What is the ignoble assembly?

This assembly which does not understand, as it truly is, that "this is the noble truth of suffering," and does not understand, as it truly is, that "this is the origin of suffering, this is the cessation of suffering, and this is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering—
the noble truth"— is called a non-noble assembly.

(EĀ.Trip 26.73) What is the noble assembly? It is that assembly which understands, as it truly is, that "this is the noble truth of suffering"; and which understands, as it truly is, that "this is the origin of suffering," "this is the cessation of suffering," and "this is the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering."
This is called the noble assembly.
As for what I said—that I would teach you both the ignoble assembly and the noble assembly—this is my response to that.

Dharma, Vinaya, offense, heavy [offense], with remainder, practiced, not spoken, not prescribed, not designated, not brought together.
