the first is the introduction; the training is to be explained next; and the last concerns what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma.
The summary verse:
By means of twenty-seven factors, one should practice the nine knowledges;
[these concern] view, conventional truth, protection, the *kiṃpuruṣa*, and the *poṣadha*.
The bowl is for the purpose of requesting almsfood.
Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery.
There the Blessed One addressed the monks:
Two dharmas: name and form; ignorance and craving for existence;
the view of eternalism and the view of annihilationism.
Lack of shame and lack of dread;
shame and dread;
being difficult to speak with and having evil friends.
Being easy to speak with and being a virtuous friend; skill regarding transgressions and skill regarding emergence from transgressions;
skill regarding meditative attainments and skill regarding emergence from meditative attainments.
Skill in the elements and skill in mental attention;
uprightness and gentleness;
patience and mildness.
Friendliness and hospitality;
mindfulness and clear comprehension;
the power of analytical reflection and the power of cultivation.
Not guarding the doors of the sense faculties and lack of moderation in eating;
guarding the doors of the sense faculties and moderation in eating;
failure in ethical discipline and failure in right view.
The ruin of ethical discipline and the ruin of view;
the perfection of ethical discipline and the perfection of view;
the purity of ethical discipline and the purity of view.

Purity of view, and likewise the fundamental application toward that which has not yet been seen; a sense of spiritual urgency regarding those things that inspire urgency, and likewise the fundamental application for one who feels such urgency; lack of contentment with regard to wholesome qualities, and non-desistance in the practice of abandonment.
Calm abiding and insight;
knowledge and liberation.
Intermediate Summary:
Two dharmas are name and form; ignorance is the second item;
the view of existence, lack of shame, shame, and also difficult speech.
Ease of speech, as well as transgression and attainment, the realms, uprightness, patience, amiability, mindfulness, the powers, the faculties, and ethical discipline.
Success, misfortune, prosperity, and the two [factors] for purity; spiritual urgency, lack of complacency, tranquility, knowledge, and wisdom—these belong to the one who knows.
There are two knowledges:
the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*). Likewise, there are the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) and conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
The knowledge of suffering and the knowledge of its origin;
the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path;
the dharma-knowledge regarding suffering and the subsequent knowledge regarding suffering.
Knowledge of phenomena regarding origination and subsequent knowledge regarding origination; knowledge of phenomena regarding cessation and subsequent knowledge regarding cessation;
knowledge of phenomena regarding the path and subsequent knowledge regarding the path.
The knowledge of destruction and the knowledge of non-arising.
There are two causes and two conditions for the arising of right view:
the voice of another and internal wise attention.
There are two truths:
conventional truth and ultimate truth.
(EĀ.Trip 28.5) Regarding these two factors—truth and the unshakable—one must apply oneself to intense mental protection, mindfulness, and heedfulness.
(EĀ.Trip 28.61) Perceiving two purposes, the *kiṃpuruṣa* does not utter *kiṃpuruṣī* speech:
"May I not commit false speech, and may I not cause others to experience grief and dejection through what is untrue.
(EĀ.Trip 28.62) Perceiving these very same two purposes, the true person (*satpuruṣa*) does not utter *kiṃpuruṣī* speech.
I shall not speak falsehood, nor shall I cause others to experience grief and dejection through what is untrue.
There are two *poṣadha* days:
the fourteenth and the fifteenth.
There are two times for entering the rains retreat:
the earlier and the later.
[One] leaf is missing.

There are two alms-meals that are exactly equal in their maturation (*vipāka*): the alms-meal having consumed which the Bodhisattva fully awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment (*anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi*), and the alms-meal having consumed which the Tathāgata [entered] the realm of Nirvana without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa*).
And he has attained final nirvana in the realm of nirvana.
(EĀ.Trip 28.Z1) There are two matters regarding a monk’s petition.
A monk, petitioning correctly, should petition thus: "O, may I become such as these, namely the monks Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana!
Why is that?
For this, monks, is the measure, this is the standard for my disciples among the monks, namely the two monks Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana.
There are two matters concerning the formal request of a nun: a nun, making a formal request correctly, should request thus: "Oh, may I become such as Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī or the nun Utpalavarṇā!"
For what reason?
Monks, this indeed is the standard, this is the measure for my female disciples, the bhikṣuṇīs: namely, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī or the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā.
There are two matters of request for a lay follower.
A lay follower who makes a request in this way should petition thus: "O, may I become such as the householder Anāthapiṇḍada is at Śrāvastī, or as Hastaka Āḷavaka is at Kauśāmbī!
Why is that?
Monks, this indeed is the standard, this is the measure for my lay disciple followers: namely, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada at Śrāvastī and Hastaka Āḷavaka at Kauśāmbī.

(EĀ.Trip 28.Z4) There are two matters for a female lay follower to request. A female lay follower, requesting correctly, should request thus: "O, may I become such as Viśākhā Mṛgāramātā in Śrāvastī, or Kubjottarā in Kauśāmbī.
And for what reason?
For this indeed, monks, is the standard, this is the measure for my female lay disciples (upāsikā), namely: Viśākhā Mṛgāramātā in Śrāvastī, and Kubjottarā in Kauśāmbī.
Summary verse:
The five gates, gain,
the four [factors], tranquility, greed, and wisdom— this is the section on the trainee (śaikṣa).
Two qualities are of great benefit to one in training (*śaikṣa*):
shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*vyapatrāpya*).
Likewise, being easy to speak with (*suvacatva*) and having virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitratā*).
Skill in offenses and skill in emerging from offenses;
skill in meditative attainments and skill in emerging from meditative attainments;
skill in the elements and skill in mental attention.
Uprightness and gentleness; patience and mildness; amiability and hospitality.
Mindfulness and clear comprehension;
the power of discernment and the power of cultivation;
guarding the doors of the sense faculties and moderation in eating.
The perfection of ethical discipline and the perfection of view;
the purity of ethical discipline and the purity of view;
and the thorough application of right effort toward such a purified view and that which is not yet seen.
A sense of spiritual urgency regarding things that inspire urgency; for one thus stirred, the application of proper attention;
lack of contentment with regard to wholesome qualities and non-desistance from abandonment;
and both calm abiding and insight.
Knowledge and liberation.

the knowledge of phenomena and subsequent knowledge; likewise, the knowledge of others' minds and conventional knowledge.

the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path;
and the dharma-knowledge regarding suffering and the subsequent knowledge regarding suffering.
The knowledge of phenomena regarding cessation and the subsequent knowledge regarding cessation;
the knowledge of phenomena regarding the path and the subsequent knowledge regarding the path.

the voice of another and wise attention within oneself.
(EĀ.Trip 29.4) Two truths are of great benefit to one in training:
conventional truth and ultimate truth.
(EĀ.Trip 29.5) Regarding two things, a trainee should apply himself with intense mental protection, mindfulness, and heedfulness: namely, to the truths and to the unshakable state.
(EĀ.Trip 29.6) Two qualities are of great benefit to one in training:
mindfulness established with regard to the body, and not casting the eyes about when inside a house.
(EĀ.Trip 29.7) Two qualities are of great benefit to one in training.
And delight in the homeless life.

he is led astray by gain and is discouraged by lack of gain.
(EĀ.Trip 29.82) Two qualities lead to the non-decline of a trainee: [he is not led astray by gain and is not discouraged by lack of gain].
One is not led astray by gain, nor is one thwarted by loss;
as it is with gain and loss, so it is with fame and infamy, blame and praise, pleasure and pain.
(EĀ.Trip 29.91) Two qualities lead to the abandonment of passion for one in training:
serenity and insight.
(EĀ.Trip 29.92) Two qualities lead to the abandonment of greed for one in training.
Calm abiding and insight.
Just as with greed, so it is with hatred and delusion, as previously written.

Calm abiding and insight.

One should have the faculties, powers, and factors of enlightenment fashioned from ten parts.

Unrighteous conduct and improper conduct arise in the world for the harm of many people, for the suffering of many people, for the disadvantage, harm, and suffering of gods and humans.

The practice of Dharma and the practice of equanimity arise in the world for the welfare of many people, for the happiness of many people, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans.

For whatever various kinds of evil, unwholesome states arise, they all have unrighteous conduct and uneven conduct as their root.

(EĀ.Trip 30.22) Whatever various kinds of wholesome states arise, they all have righteous conduct and even conduct as their root; they originate from righteous conduct and even conduct, are born of righteous conduct and even conduct, and are produced by righteous conduct and even conduct.
For, monks, whatever various kinds of wholesome states arise, they all have righteous conduct and even conduct as their root.
Two things lead to misfortune: unrighteous conduct and uneven conduct. Two things lead to welfare: righteous conduct and even conduct.

Just as for what is disadvantageous and for what is advantageous, so too for what is harmful and for what is beneficial, for suffering and for happiness, for calamity and for prosperity, for misfortune and for success, for lack of accomplishment and for accomplishment,
for non-fulfillment and for fulfillment, and for decline and for non-decline.
For the sake of falling away.

For the sake of what is beneficial in this present life, for the sake of what is not beneficial in this present life; for the sake of what is beneficial in future lives, for the sake of what is not beneficial in future lives.

(EĀ.Trip 30.41) By two factors, unarisen evil and unwholesome states arise; that is to say, by unrighteous conduct (*adharmacaryā*) and by uneven conduct (*viṣamacaryā*). Through unrighteous conduct and uneven conduct, unarisen evil and unwholesome states arise. (EĀ.Trip 30.42) By two factors, unarisen evil and unwholesome states do not arise; that is to say, by righteous conduct (*dharmacaryā*) and by even conduct (*samacaryā*).
Through righteous conduct and even conduct, unarisen evil and unwholesome states do not arise.
Through two factors, unarisen wholesome states do not arise; namely, through unrighteous conduct and uneven conduct.
Through unrighteous conduct and uneven conduct, unarisen wholesome states do not arise.
(EĀ.Trip 30.44) By means of two qualities, unarisen wholesome states arise; that is to say, by the practice of the Dharma and by even conduct.
Through the practice of the Dharma and through even conduct, unarisen wholesome states arise.

Through unrighteous conduct and through uneven conduct, unarisen evil and unwholesome states arise, and those already arisen increase, grow, and reach full expansion.
By means of two things, however, unarisen evil and unwholesome states do not arise, and those already arisen are abandoned; namely, through righteous conduct and through even conduct.
Through righteous conduct and even conduct, unarisen evil and unwholesome states do not arise, and those already arisen are abandoned.
(EĀ.Trip 30.47) By two factors, unarisen wholesome states do not arise and those already arisen are abandoned; namely, through unrighteous conduct and uneven conduct.
Through unrighteous conduct and uneven conduct, unarisen wholesome states do not arise and those already arisen are abandoned.

(EĀ.Trip 30.48) By means of two qualities, unarisen wholesome states arise, and those already arisen attain further increase, growth, and expansion; namely, through the practice of the Dharma and through even conduct.
Through the practice of the Dharma and through even conduct, unarisen wholesome states arise, and those already arisen attain further increase, growth, and expansion.
[Gap] (EĀ.Trip 32.201) Two things lead to passion: unrighteous conduct and uneven conduct. Unrighteous conduct and uneven conduct lead to passion.
"Two qualities lead to non-attachment: the practice of Dharma and the practice of equanimity. The practice of Dharma and the practice of equanimity lead to non-attachment.
Thus he spoke.
Just as they lead to passion and the absence of passion, so too do they lead to hatred and the absence of hatred; to delusion and the absence of delusion;
to bondage and liberation; to affliction and purification; to accumulation and diminution; to grasping and non-grasping;
to annihilation and non-annihilation; to coagulation and dispersion; to thickening and clearing away; and to abundance.

"They lead to both austerity and social contact, to non-contact and conceptual proliferation, to the absence of proliferation, to a dwelling place and the absence of a dwelling place, and to lack of tranquility and tranquility.
Thus he spoke.

(EĀ.Trip 32.301) Two things lead to dispassion: namely, unrighteous conduct and uneven conduct. Unrighteous conduct and uneven conduct lead to dispassion. Two things lead to attainment: righteous conduct and even conduct.
"Both the practice of the Dharma and the practice of equanimity lead to its fulfillment.
Thus he spoke.

Just as for dispassion and passion, so too for contentment and discontent, for causing blindness and not causing blindness, for causing loss of sight and causing sight, for causing ignorance and causing knowledge, for the weakness of wisdom and the increase of wisdom, for the side of affliction and the side of non-affliction, for lack of direct knowledge and direct knowledge, for lack of full awakening and full awakening... [and so forth].
This he said.
Two things lead to misconduct: unrighteous conduct and uneven conduct. Unrighteous conduct and uneven conduct lead to misconduct. Two things lead to good conduct: righteous conduct and even conduct.
"Practice of the Dharma and practice of equanimity lead to good conduct.
Thus he spoke.

Just as with misconduct and good conduct, so it is with the unwholesome and the wholesome; the blameworthy and the blameless; the censurable and the uncensurable; the harmful and the harmless; that which is accompanied by remorse and that which is without remorse; that which is accompanied by reproach and that which is without reproach; that which is contrary and that which is conformable; the inappropriate and the appropriate.
"Regarding that which is not a means and that which is a means, that which is improper and that which is proper... [he] said this.

Two things lead to the inferior: unrighteous conduct and uneven conduct; unrighteous conduct and uneven conduct lead to the inferior. Two things lead to the sublime: righteous conduct and even conduct.
"Practice of the Dharma and practice of equanimity lead to the sublime.
Thus he spoke.
Just as with the inferior and the sublime, so it is with the dark and the bright... [and] that which leads to the higher realms;

with wrong view and right view, wrong practice and right practice, wrong resolve and right resolve... [and] misfortune and prosperity, lack of wisdom and the perfection of wisdom, and loss of mindfulness.
For the sake of established mindfulness; for that which leads away from concentration and for that which leads toward concentration; for ignorance and for knowledge;

Two things lead to association with wholesome persons: righteous conduct and even conduct.
"Practice of the Dharma and practice of equanimity lead to the service of true persons.

(EĀ.Trip 32.701) Two qualities lead to a lack of respect for the Buddha: unrighteous conduct and uneven conduct. Unrighteous conduct and uneven conduct lead to a lack of respect for the Buddha. Two qualities lead to respect for the Buddha: righteous conduct and even conduct.
"Practice of the Dharma and practice of equanimity lead to reverence for the Buddha.
Thus he spoke.
As it is with respect to lack of reverence and reverence, so it is with respect to lack of deference and proper deference;
as it is with respect to the Buddha, so it is with respect to the Dharma, the Saṅgha, the training, the instruction, heedfulness, hospitality, and meditative concentration.

Two things do not lead to being filial toward one's mother: unrighteous conduct and uneven conduct. [Conversely,] unrighteous conduct and uneven conduct do lead to being filial toward one's mother. Two things lead to being filial toward one's mother: righteous conduct and even conduct.
"Practice of the Dharma and practice of equanimity lead to being filial toward one's mother.
Thus he spoke.

Just as he does not attain what is for the sake of being filial toward one's mother, nor what is for the sake of being filial toward one's father; nor for the sake of being a *śramaṇa*, nor what is for the sake of being a *śramaṇa*;

nor for the sake of being a *brāhmaṇa*, nor what is for the sake of being a *brāhmaṇa*; nor for the sake of honoring the elders in the family, nor what is for the sake of honoring the elders in the family;
[he does not attain] great desire, little desire, [and so forth]... [nor] being difficult to support, nor what is for the sake of being easy to support—he becomes a possessor [of these].

He is one who, for the sake of great desire, becomes a seeker of gain; yet he dwells without contentment regarding robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, while he also dwells with contentment regarding robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
